en.title: Electrical and Electronic Engineering: the whole course
en.short: What electrical and electronic engineering covers, how the course is organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What electrical and electronic engineering is
sections.text:
Electrical and electronic engineering is the study of how electricity is generated, moved, controlled and used, and how electronic circuits carry and process information. Electrical engineering usually deals with power: generators, transformers, transmission lines, machines, drives and installations. Electronic engineering usually deals with signals and information: diodes, transistors, amplifiers, digital logic, microcontrollers, communication and control. Most degree courses combine both, because modern power systems also depend on electronics and computing.

The subject rests on mathematics, physics, circuit theory, materials and measurement. It matters because reliable electricity and electronic systems support health care, transport, industry and communication. A fault can injure people or stop essential services.

These summaries teach principles. They do not replace a design code, a standard or a qualified engineer. Codes, standards and registration rules differ by country. In Nigeria, COREN registers engineers. Other countries have their own bodies and laws. Check the current official source before you design or install anything.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, a BEng usually takes five years and includes industrial training under SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme. Polytechnic students commonly take an ND, then supervised industrial work, then an HND. In the UK, a BEng usually takes three years and an MEng four; in Scotland each usually takes a year longer. Ghana and Kenya have their own degree and diploma patterns. Always check your own handbook.

The early years are usually shared with other engineering students: mathematics, physics, basic circuits, programming, measurement and laboratory practice. Later years add power, electronics, control, communication and design. Most courses include laboratory work, a group design project and an individual final-year project. A master’s degree adds advanced analysis, research methods and a dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
Teaching usually begins with engineering mathematics: calculus and series, complex numbers and phasors, linear algebra and differential equations. These support DC circuit analysis, network theorems, electromagnetism and fields, electrical materials and components, digital logic design, measurement and instrumentation, and programming with numerical methods.

The core then covers AC circuit analysis and three-phase power, semiconductor devices and diodes, transistors and amplifiers, operational amplifiers and analogue design, digital systems and microcontrollers, signals and systems, and control systems. Power subjects follow: transformers, rotating machines, power electronics and drives, power systems analysis and protection, and electrical installation design and regulations. Communication systems and electromagnetic waves, digital signal processing, renewable energy and distributed generation, and professional practice, ethics and project management complete the core.

At master’s level, common topics are advanced power systems analysis and stability, advanced control systems, advanced electromagnetic theory and computational methods, and research methods with a dissertation. The order varies, but the logic is steady: tools first, then devices and circuits, then systems, then application and design.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Solve problems by hand before using software. Draw the circuit or block diagram, label nodes, currents, voltages and reference directions, then write the equations. Keep units on every line and convert prefixes before calculating. Ask whether the answer is reasonable: a small signal should not need a huge supply, and a cable should not carry far more current than its size allows.

Learn typical values and the conditions behind each formula. Use simulation to check your hand result, not to replace it. In the laboratory, connect circuits safely, measure before you trust, and record what you did. Build small low-voltage circuits only under supervision. Study mathematics steadily, because later subjects reuse it. Work through past questions and explain your method aloud. Work in groups, but write solutions alone.

sections.heading: Common mistakes students make
sections.text:
Common mistakes include mixing units, ignoring sign conventions, confusing peak and root-mean-square values, and forgetting phase differences in AC work. Students also treat ideal op-amp assumptions as always true, ignore transistor bias, or copy a formula without checking its conditions.

Other errors are trusting simulation output because it looks precise, using a logic level that the device does not accept, and writing code without testing small parts. In power and installation work, never guess a protective device rating or a cable size. Follow the current local regulations and let a qualified person check the design.

Finally, state assumptions and show the method. An examiner needs to see how you reached the answer, not only the answer.

keyPoints: Electrical engineering deals mainly with power, while electronic engineering deals mainly with signals and information.
Degree length, awards and registration differ by country, so check your handbook and the current official body.
Study the mathematical tools first, then devices and circuits, then systems and applications.
Draw diagrams, keep units, and check every answer for reasonableness.
Use simulation and software only after you understand the hand method.
Design and installation must follow the current local code and be checked by a qualified engineer.

en.title: Engineering mathematics: calculus and series
en.short: Derivatives, integrals, series, partial derivatives and maxima, with engineering applications.

sections.heading: Differentiation rules
sections.text:
The derivative is a rate of change: for y = f(x), dy/dx is the gradient of the curve. Standard results include d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹, d/dx(sin x) = cos x and d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ.

Three rules combine them. Product rule: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′. Quotient rule: (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v². Chain rule: dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx.

Example: y = x² sin 3x gives dy/dx = 2x sin 3x + 3x² cos 3x.

sections.heading: Integration and area
sections.text:
Integration reverses differentiation: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C for n ≠ −1, and ∫cos x dx = sin x + C. A definite integral gives the area under a curve.

Example: the area under y = 3x² + 2x from x = 0 to x = 2.
∫₀²(3x² + 2x)dx = [x³ + x²]₀² = 12 square units.

With no simple antiderivative, the trapezium rule approximates the area: h/2 × [first + last + 2 × (sum of middle ordinates)], h being the strip width.

sections.heading: Sequences and series
sections.text:
A sequence is an ordered list of terms; a series is their sum. An arithmetic series has a constant difference d, so the nth term is a + (n−1)d. A geometric series has a constant ratio r, so the nth term is arⁿ⁻¹ and the sum to infinity is a/(1−r), valid only when |r| < 1.

Power series expand functions: eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2! + …, sin x = x − x³/3! + … They allow numerical evaluation and linearisation for small changes.

sections.heading: Partial derivatives and maxima
sections.text:
If z = f(x, y), the partial derivative ∂z/∂x treats y as constant. At a stationary point both ∂z/∂x and ∂z/∂y are zero. The test D = (∂²z/∂x²)(∂²z/∂y²) − (∂²z/∂x∂y)² decides: D > 0 with ∂²z/∂x² > 0 is a minimum, D > 0 with ∂²z/∂x² < 0 a maximum, D < 0 a saddle point.

For one variable, solve dy/dx = 0 and check the sign of d²y/dx².

keyPoints: dy/dx measures the rate of change; d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹, d/dx(sin x) = cos x, d/dx(eˣ) = eˣ.
Product rule (uv)′ = u′v + uv′; quotient rule (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²; chain rule dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx.
A definite integral gives the area under a curve, and integration reverses differentiation, with + C for indefinite integrals.
The sum to infinity of a geometric series is a/(1−r), valid only when |r| < 1.
For z = f(x, y), set ∂z/∂x = ∂z/∂y = 0 and use D = (∂²z/∂x²)(∂²z/∂y²) − (∂²z/∂x∂y)² to classify the point.
The trapezium rule approximates an area when no simple antiderivative exists.

en.title: Complex numbers and phasors
en.short: Complex algebra, Euler’s relation, phasors and complex impedance in simple AC circuits.

sections.heading: Complex forms
sections.text: A complex number has real and imaginary parts. In rectangular form z = a + jb, where j² = −1. Electrical engineers use j because i usually means current. On the Argand diagram, a is horizontal and b vertical. The polar form is z = r∠θ, with r = √(a² + b²) and θ = arctan(b/a), choosing the quadrant from the signs of a and b. The exponential form is z = r e^(jθ). Euler’s relation gives e^(jθ) = cos θ + j sin θ, so the forms agree. Add or subtract in rectangular form. Multiply or divide in polar form: multiply magnitudes and add angles, or divide magnitudes and subtract angles.

sections.heading: Phasors
sections.text: A sinusoid v(t) = V_m cos(ωt + φ) has amplitude V_m, angular frequency ω and phase φ. Its phasor is V = V_m∠φ. The phasor stores amplitude and phase; frequency is kept separately. It is not the instantaneous value. Differentiation with respect to time becomes multiplication by jω in the phasor domain. This turns steady sinusoidal circuit problems into algebra. Use peak or RMS values consistently; a phasor may be scaled to RMS.

sections.heading: Impedance example
sections.text: Impedance is the complex ratio Z = V ÷ I. For a resistor Z = R. For an inductor Z = jωL. For a capacitor Z = 1 ÷ (jωC) = −j ÷ (ωC). Series impedances add. Example: a 30 Ω resistor and an inductor with reactance 40 Ω are in series across V = 100∠0° V. Then Z = 30 + j40 Ω. Its magnitude is √(30² + 40²) = 50 Ω and its angle is arctan(40/30) = 53.13°. The current is I = V ÷ Z = 100∠0° ÷ 50∠53.13° = 2∠−53.13° A. The current lags the voltage by 53.13°, as expected for an inductive circuit.

keyPoints: Rectangular form is z = a + jb, with j² = −1.
Polar form is z = r∠θ, where r = √(a² + b²) and θ is the argument.
Euler’s relation: e^(jθ) = cos θ + j sin θ.
Multiply phasors by multiplying magnitudes and adding angles; divide by dividing magnitudes and subtracting angles.
A sinusoid V_m cos(ωt + φ) has phasor V = V_m∠φ at frequency ω.
Impedance is Z = V ÷ I; series impedances add, and for an inductor Z = jωL and for a capacitor Z = 1 ÷ (jωC).

en.title: Linear algebra and differential equations
en.short: Matrices, determinants, eigenvalues and linear systems, then first- and second-order ODEs in RC, RL and RLC circuits.

sections.heading: Matrices and linear systems
sections.text:
A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers; an m × n matrix has m rows and n columns. Multiplication is row times column, and AB is usually not BA. A linear system is written Ax = b, with A the coefficients, x the unknowns and b the constants. Gaussian elimination adds multiples of one row to another until the augmented matrix [A|b] is in row echelon form, then back-substitution gives the unknowns. A unique solution needs independent rows; otherwise there are none or infinitely many.

Example: 2x + y = 5 and x − y = 1. Adding the equations gives 3x = 6, so x = 2 and y = 1.

sections.heading: Determinants and eigenvalues
sections.text:
The determinant of [[a, b], [c, d]] is ad − bc. A square matrix has an inverse only if its determinant is non-zero, and then A⁻¹ = adj(A) ÷ det(A), where adj(A) is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. The system then has solution x = A⁻¹b.

An eigenvalue λ and eigenvector v satisfy Av = λv, found from det(A − λI) = 0. For A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]], (2 − λ)² − 1 = 0 gives λ = 1 and λ = 3. Eigenvalues describe the natural modes of a circuit or control system.

sections.heading: First-order equations
sections.text:
A first-order linear equation dy/dt + ay = f(t) has solution y = y_p + K e^(−at), where y_p is any particular solution, τ = 1/a is the time constant and K is fixed by the initial condition.

For an RC circuit, R dq/dt + q/C = V gives τ = RC and, charging from zero, q = CV(1 − e^(−t/RC)). For an RL circuit, L di/dt + Ri = V gives τ = L/R and i = (V/R)(1 − e^(−Rt/L)).

sections.heading: Second-order equations
sections.text:
For ay″ + by′ + cy = f(t), solve the characteristic equation aλ² + bλ + c = 0. Distinct real roots give two exponentials; a repeated root gives (K₁ + K₂t)e^(λt); complex roots α ± jβ give e^(αt)(K₁ cos βt + K₂ sin βt).

A series RLC circuit obeys L d²i/dt² + R di/dt + i/C = 0, so λ = (−R ± √(R² − 4L/C)) ÷ 2L. The damping ratio ζ = (R/2)√(C/L) gives an overdamped (ζ > 1), critically damped (ζ = 1) or underdamped (ζ < 1) response.

keyPoints: A linear system Ax = b is solved by Gaussian elimination, or by x = A⁻¹b when A is invertible.
A square matrix is invertible only if det(A) ≠ 0; eigenvalues come from det(A − λI) = 0.
First-order solution: y = y_p + K e^(−at), with time constant τ = 1/a.
RC circuit: τ = RC. RL circuit: τ = L/R.
Second-order response depends on the roots of aλ² + bλ + c = 0: real, repeated or complex.
For a series RLC circuit, ζ = (R/2)√(C/L) sets overdamped, critical or underdamped behaviour.

en.title: DC circuit analysis
en.short: Charge, current, voltage, power, Ohm and Kirchhoff laws, dividers, source transformation and RC/RL transients.

sections.heading: Quantities and power
sections.text: Charge Q is measured in coulombs (C). Current I is the rate of charge flow, I = Q ÷ t, in amperes (A). Voltage V is energy per unit charge, in volts (V). Resistance R is opposition to current, in ohms (Ω). Power P is the rate of energy transfer, P = VI = I²R = V² ÷ R, in watts (W).

sections.heading: Ohm and Kirchhoff
sections.text: Ohm’s law relates the three for a linear resistor: V = IR. Kirchhoff’s current law says the currents entering a node equal those leaving. Kirchhoff’s voltage law says the signed voltages around a closed loop sum to zero. These laws hold for any circuit and are the basis of all DC analysis.

sections.heading: Series, parallel, dividers
sections.text:
Resistances in series add: Rtotal = R1 + R2 + ... For parallel resistances, 1 ÷ Rtotal = 1 ÷ R1 + 1 ÷ R2 + ... A series voltage divider gives Vx = Vs × Rx ÷ Rtotal. A current divider between two parallel resistors gives I1 = Is × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2). Source transformation replaces a voltage source Vs in series with R by a current source Is = Vs ÷ R in parallel with R, and the reverse.

Example: 12 V across 6 Ω and 3 Ω in series. Rtotal = 9 Ω, I = 12 ÷ 9 = 1.33 A, V across 3 Ω = 12 × 3 ÷ 9 = 4 V, total power = 12 × 1.33 = 16 W.

sections.heading: Capacitors and inductors
sections.text: A capacitor stores charge and opposes change in voltage. In a simple resistor-capacitor (RC) circuit with a constant source, vC = Vs(1 − e^(−t÷τ)), where τ = RC is the time constant. An inductor opposes change in current. In a simple resistor-inductor (RL) circuit, i = (Vs ÷ R)(1 − e^(−t÷τ)), where τ = L ÷ R is the time constant. After about five time constants the change is almost complete.

keyPoints: Current is charge flow, I = Q ÷ t; power is P = VI = I²R = V² ÷ R.
Ohm’s law for a linear resistor is V = IR.
Kirchhoff’s laws: currents at a node sum to zero, and voltages around a loop sum to zero.
Series resistances add; parallel conductances add, so 1 ÷ Rtotal = Σ(1 ÷ Ri).
Voltage divider Vx = Vs Rx ÷ Rtotal; current divider I1 = Is R2 ÷ (R1 + R2).
RC and RL time constants are τ = RC and τ = L ÷ R; capacitor voltage and inductor current change exponentially.

en.title: Network theorems and analysis methods
en.short: Nodal and mesh analysis, superposition, Thevenin, Norton, maximum power and network transformations.

sections.heading: Nodal and mesh
sections.text:
Nodal analysis applies Kirchhoff’s current law at each node: currents leaving a node sum to zero. Pick a reference node, assign node voltages, solve. Mesh analysis applies Kirchhoff’s voltage law around independent loops and solves for loop currents. Use nodal for many parallel branches, mesh for many series branches.

Example: 12 V across 4 Ω and 6 Ω in series gives I = 12 ÷ (4 + 6) = 1.2 A.

sections.heading: Superposition
sections.text:
Superposition applies to linear circuits with several independent sources. Switch off all but one, find its contribution, then add. A switched-off voltage source is a short circuit; a switched-off current source is an open circuit. Superposition does not apply to power.

Source transformation replaces V in series with R by V ÷ R in parallel with R, and the reverse.

sections.heading: Thevenin and Norton
sections.text:
Thevenin’s theorem replaces a linear two-terminal network by Vth in series with Rth. Vth is the open-circuit voltage; Rth is the resistance seen with sources switched off. Norton’s equivalent is In = Vth ÷ Rth in parallel with Rth. Maximum power transfer occurs when load resistance equals Rth, giving Pmax = Vth² ÷ (4Rth).

Example: Vth = 12 V, Rth = 4 Ω, load 6 Ω. Load current = 12 ÷ (4 + 6) = 1.2 A; load voltage = 7.2 V. At load 4 Ω, Pmax = 144 ÷ 16 = 9 W.

sections.heading: Reciprocity and transformations
sections.text:
Reciprocity: in a linear bilateral network, a voltage source in one branch causing current in another gives the same current in the first when moved to the second. Substitution replaces a branch by an ideal voltage source equal to the voltage across the branch, or an ideal current source equal to the current through the branch, leaving currents and voltages elsewhere unchanged.

Delta-star conversion changes three resistors in a triangle to three joined at a centre. For delta resistances Rab, Rbc, Rca, star resistance at node a is Ra = (Rab × Rca) ÷ (Rab + Rbc + Rca).

keyPoints: Nodal analysis uses Kirchhoff’s current law; mesh analysis uses Kirchhoff’s voltage law.
Superposition applies only to linear circuits and not to power.
Thevenin: Vth in series with Rth; Norton: In = Vth ÷ Rth in parallel with Rth.
Maximum power transfer occurs at RL = Rth, with Pmax = Vth² ÷ (4Rth).
Delta-star: Ra = (Rab × Rca) ÷ (Rab + Rbc + Rca); star-delta: Rab = (RaRb + RbRc + RcRa) ÷ Rc.
Reciprocity holds in linear bilateral networks; substitution replaces a branch by an equivalent ideal voltage or current source.

en.title: Electromagnetism and fields
en.short: Coulomb, electric field and potential, Gauss and capacitance, magnetic fields, induction and Maxwell.

sections.heading: Electric fields
sections.text:
Coulomb’s law gives the force between point charges: F = k q1 q2 ÷ r², where k = 1 ÷ (4π ε0) ≈ 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C² in a vacuum. The electric field E is force per unit positive charge, E = F ÷ q, in N/C or V/m. Field lines point from positive to negative charge. Potential V is work per unit charge, V = W ÷ q, in volts; E = −dV ÷ dr.

Example: q1 = q2 = 1 μC at r = 0.1 m gives F = (8.99 × 10⁹ × 10⁻¹²) ÷ 0.01 = 0.899 N.

sections.heading: Gauss and capacitance
sections.text: Gauss’s law says the electric flux through a closed surface equals enclosed charge ÷ ε0: Φ = Q ÷ ε0. It helps when symmetry makes the field constant over the surface. A capacitor stores charge; capacitance is C = Q ÷ V, in farads. For a parallel-plate capacitor with area A, separation d and vacuum between, C = ε0 A ÷ d; a dielectric (insulating material) multiplies this by relative permittivity. Energy stored is ½CV².

sections.heading: Magnetic fields
sections.text: Currents produce magnetic fields. The Biot-Savart law gives the field of a small current element: dB = μ0 I dl sinθ ÷ (4π r²). Ampere’s law, ∮B·dl = μ0 I, gives the field when symmetry helps. For a long straight wire, B = μ0 I ÷ (2π r), where μ0 ≈ 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m. The field circles the wire; the right-hand rule gives its direction.

sections.heading: Induction and Maxwell
sections.text: Faraday’s law: a changing magnetic flux Φ through a circuit induces an emf (electromotive force), emf = −dΦ ÷ dt; the minus sign is Lenz’s law, opposing the change. Inductance L = Φ ÷ I, and a changing current gives emf = −L dI ÷ dt. Maxwell’s equations summarise the field laws: Gauss for E and for B (no magnetic monopoles), Ampere-Maxwell (currents and changing E make B), and Faraday (changing B makes E).

keyPoints: Coulomb’s law is F = k q1 q2 ÷ r², with k = 1 ÷ (4π ε0).
Electric field is E = F ÷ q and potential is V = W ÷ q, with E = −dV ÷ dr.
Gauss’s law is Φ = Q ÷ ε0; capacitance is C = Q ÷ V, and for a parallel-plate capacitor C = ε0 A ÷ d.
Ampere’s law is ∮B·dl = μ0 I; the Biot-Savart law is dB = μ0 I dl sinθ ÷ (4π r²).
Faraday’s law is emf = −dΦ ÷ dt, and inductance is L = Φ ÷ I.
Maxwell’s equations link changing electric and magnetic fields and include no magnetic monopoles.

en.title: Electrical materials and components
en.short: Conductors, insulators, semiconductors, magnetic materials and the passive components built from them.

sections.heading: Conductors and resistivity
sections.text:
Resistance depends on material and shape: R = ρL ÷ A, where ρ is resistivity (Ω·m), L length and A cross-sectional area. Conductors such as copper and aluminium have low ρ because many electrons are free. In metals ρ rises with temperature: ρ ≈ ρ0[1 + α(T − T0)], where α is the temperature coefficient at T0.

Example: copper wire, L = 2 m, A = 1 mm² = 1 × 10^-6 m², ρ = 1.7 × 10^-8 Ω·m at 20 °C. R = 1.7 × 10^-8 × 2 ÷ (1 × 10^-6) = 0.034 Ω. For α = 0.0039 per °C and ΔT = 50 °C, ΔR = 0.034 × 0.0039 × 50 = 0.0066 Ω, so R ≈ 0.041 Ω.

sections.heading: Insulators and semiconductors
sections.text: Insulators such as glass, rubber and ceramics have very high resistivity. They block current but break down above a limiting voltage, and heat or moisture lowers their resistance. Semiconductors such as silicon lie between conductors and insulators. Doping, adding controlled impurities, raises conductivity. Their resistance usually falls as temperature rises, a negative temperature coefficient, so devices need thermal design.

sections.heading: Magnetic materials
sections.text: Ferromagnetic materials such as iron have domains that align with an applied field, giving high permeability. They show saturation, a maximum flux density, and hysteresis, energy lost per cycle in the B-H loop. Soft magnetic materials have narrow loops and suit transformer cores; hard magnetic materials have wide loops and make permanent magnets. Eddy currents cause loss, reduced by laminating cores or using ferrites at high frequency.

sections.heading: Passive components
sections.text: Resistors use carbon film, metal film or wire. Limits are tolerance, power rating, temperature coefficient and noise; wirewound types can be inductive. Capacitors store charge, C = εA ÷ d where ε is permittivity, and come as ceramic, film or electrolytic types. Limits include voltage rating, leakage, equivalent series resistance and, for electrolytics, polarity. Inductors are coils, often with magnetic cores; limits include winding resistance, saturation and self-resonance. Transformer cores use laminated silicon steel at mains frequency and ferrites at high frequency to limit eddy and hysteresis loss.

keyPoints: Resistance is R = ρL ÷ A, and resistivity is a material property.
Metals have a positive temperature coefficient, while semiconductors usually have a negative one.
Insulators have high resistivity but finite breakdown strength.
Soft magnetic materials suit transformer cores; hard magnetic materials make permanent magnets.
Capacitance is C = εA ÷ d, and capacitor limits include voltage rating, leakage and equivalent series resistance.
Inductor and transformer core limits include saturation, hysteresis and eddy-current loss.

en.title: Digital logic design: bits, gates and memory
en.short: Number systems, Boolean algebra, gates, Karnaugh maps, adders, multiplexers, decoders and flip-flops.

sections.heading: Number systems
sections.text:
Digital circuits use two voltage levels, so numbers are written in base 2 (binary). Each binary digit is a bit. Four bits form one hexadecimal digit (base 16).

To convert 1011 0110 to decimal, add place values: 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 182. The same bits are B6 in hexadecimal: 1011 = B (11) and 0110 = 6.

Binary-coded decimal (BCD) stores each decimal digit as four bits; BCD is not pure binary.

sections.heading: Boolean algebra and gates
sections.text:
Boolean algebra uses variables that are 0 or 1. The operations are AND (·), OR (+) and NOT (prime). Identities such as A + 0 = A, A · 1 = A, A + A' = 1 and A · A' = 0 simplify expressions.

A logic gate performs one operation. A truth table lists the output for every input combination; two inputs give four rows.

De Morgan’s laws are (A · B)' = A' + B' and (A + B)' = A' · B'.

sections.heading: Karnaugh maps
sections.text:
A Karnaugh map (K-map) arranges truth-table rows so neighbouring cells differ in one bit. Group 1s in rectangles of 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on, with wraparound at the edges. Each group removes variables that change.

Example: F = Σm(0,1) for inputs A,B has two adjacent 1s in the row A = 0, so F = A'. Check: when A = 0, F = 1 for either B; when A = 1, F = 0.

sections.heading: Blocks and memory
sections.text:
Combinational circuits have outputs that depend only on present inputs. A half adder adds two bits: sum S = A XOR B and carry C = A · B. A full adder accepts a carry-in. A multiplexer selects one of several inputs with select lines. A decoder turns a binary code into one active output line.

Sequential circuits store state. A latch is level-sensitive; a flip-flop is edge-triggered. The D flip-flop copies D to Q on a clock edge.

keyPoints: In binary, place values double from right to left; 1011 0110 = 182 = B6 in hexadecimal.
Boolean identities such as A + A' = 1 and A · A' = 0, plus De Morgan’s laws, simplify logic expressions.
A truth table lists every input combination and its output; two inputs give four rows.
In a Karnaugh map, group adjacent 1s in sizes 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on to remove changing variables.
A half adder gives S = A XOR B and C = A · B; a full adder also takes a carry-in.
A multiplexer selects one input, a decoder activates one output line, a latch is level-sensitive and a flip-flop is edge-triggered.

en.title: Engineering measurement and instrumentation
en.short: SI units, errors and uncertainty, meters, the oscilloscope, bridges and sensors.

sections.heading: Units and errors
sections.text:
The SI has seven base units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. Derived units combine them. Convert readings to coherent units before calculating.

Error is the difference from the true value. Systematic error shifts every reading the same way, such as a zero offset. Random error scatters readings and falls by averaging. Accuracy is closeness to truth; precision is closeness of repeats. Uncertainty is a stated interval. Type A comes from repeats, Type B from specifications; combine as u_c = √(u_A² + u_B²) and quote U = k u_c. Calibration compares an instrument with a traceable standard.

sections.heading: Meters and oscilloscope
sections.text:
Analogue meters show a pointer on a scale. A moving-coil meter responds to average current and its resistance loads the circuit. Digital meters use an ADC and show a number. Accuracy is often quoted as a percentage of reading plus counts, so check both. High input impedance reduces loading.

The oscilloscope plots voltage against time. The vertical control sets volts per division; the timebase sets seconds per division. The trigger stabilises the trace. A 10× probe divides voltage by ten and raises input impedance. Bandwidth limits fast signals.

sections.heading: Bridge circuits
sections.text:
A Wheatstone bridge finds an unknown resistance by balancing two dividers. With ratio arms R1 and R2, known R3 and unknown Rx, balance gives R1/R2 = R3/Rx, so Rx = R2 R3 / R1.

Example: R1 = 100 Ω, R2 = 200 Ω, R3 = 300 Ω. Rx = 200 × 300 ÷ 100 = 600 Ω. Check: 100/200 = 0.5 and 300/600 = 0.5.

AC bridges extend the idea. The Maxwell bridge measures inductance; the Schering bridge measures capacitance and loss. Some balances depend on frequency.

sections.heading: Sensors and transducers
sections.text: A sensor responds to a physical quantity; a transducer converts energy from one form to another. Examples include the strain gauge, thermistor, thermocouple, LVDT and Hall sensor. Signal conditioning amplifies, filters and converts the output. Choose a sensor for range, sensitivity, linearity, response time and environment.

keyPoints: The seven SI base units are metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela.
Systematic error shifts all readings; random error scatters them and is reduced by averaging.
Combined standard uncertainty is u_c = √(u_A² + u_B²), and expanded uncertainty is U = k u_c.
A Wheatstone bridge balances when R1/R2 = R3/Rx, so Rx = R2 R3 / R1.
An oscilloscope vertical scale is in volts per division and its timebase in seconds per division.
Calibration compares an instrument with a traceable standard and records corrections.

en.title: Programming and numerical methods for engineers
en.short: Structured programming in C or Python, with root finding, interpolation, integration and linear equations.

sections.heading: Programs and data
sections.text: A program is a list of instructions a computer follows. In C or Python, a variable names a stored value, such as voltage 12.0. Control flow chooses paths: if tests a condition, while repeats while true, and for repeats a fixed number of times. A function groups statements under a name and returns a result, so code can be reused and tested. An array, or list in Python, stores many values under one name, indexed from 0. These four ideas are the base of engineering scripts.

sections.heading: Finding roots
sections.text: A root is a value of x where f(x)=0. Bisection brackets a root between a and b with f(a) and f(b) of opposite signs, then halves the interval. Newton-Raphson uses the tangent: x(n+1) = x(n) − f(x(n)) ÷ f′(x(n)). It is faster but needs a derivative and a good start. Example: solve x² − 2 = 0 from x0 = 1. f′(x)=2x. x1 = 1 − (−1) ÷ 2 = 1.5. x2 = 1.5 − (0.25) ÷ 3 = 1.416667.

sections.heading: Interpolation and integration
sections.text: Interpolation estimates values between known points. Linear interpolation joins two points with a straight line. Numerical integration estimates the area under a curve. The trapezoidal rule with step h is ∫ f(x) dx ≈ h/2 [f0 + 2f1 + ... + 2f(n−1) + fn]. Example: f(x)=x² on [0,1] with h=0.5 gives 0.25[0 + 2(0.25) + 1] = 0.375; exact value 1/3 ≈ 0.3333. Simpson’s rule is often more accurate for smooth curves.

sections.heading: Linear equations
sections.text: Many engineering models give simultaneous linear equations. Gaussian elimination removes unknowns by row operations, then back-substitution finds them. Example: 2x + y = 5 and x + 3y = 6. Subtract half the first row from the second: 2.5y = 3.5, so y = 1.4. Then 2x + 1.4 = 5, so x = 1.8. Check: 1.8 + 3(1.4) = 6.0. Always check by substitution.

keyPoints: Variables store values, control flow chooses paths, functions reuse code and arrays hold many values.
Bisection needs a sign change; Newton-Raphson uses x(n+1) = x(n) − f(x(n)) ÷ f′(x(n)).
Linear interpolation: y = y0 + (x − x0)(y1 − y0) ÷ (x1 − x0).
Trapezoidal rule: integral of f(x) dx ≈ h/2 [f0 + 2f1 + ... + 2f(n−1) + fn].
Gaussian elimination solves linear equations by forward elimination and back-substitution.
Always check a numerical answer by substitution, by a smaller step, or by a residual.

en.title: AC circuit analysis and three-phase power
en.short: Phasors and impedance, resonance, AC power and power factor correction, and balanced three-phase systems.

sections.heading: Impedance and phasors
sections.text: In sinusoidal steady state voltages and currents share one frequency, so a phasor represents them as a complex number with magnitude and phase. A component has complex impedance, the ratio V/I: resistor R, inductor jωL, capacitor 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC), where ω = 2πf. Series impedances add; parallel impedances combine like resistors. Ohm’s law becomes V = IZ, and the angle of Z gives the phase difference between voltage and current.

sections.heading: Resonance and response
sections.text: Resonance occurs when inductive and capacitive reactances cancel. For a series RLC circuit f₀ = 1 ÷ (2π√(LC)). At resonance Z = R, current is maximum and voltage and current are in phase. The quality factor Q = (1 ÷ R)√(L ÷ C) measures sharpness; high Q means a narrow bandwidth B = f₀ ÷ Q. Frequency response plots show gain and phase against frequency.

sections.heading: Power and correction
sections.text: Real power P (watts) does useful work: P = VI cos φ for rms, where cos φ is power factor. Reactive power Q (var) is exchanged by inductors and capacitors. Apparent power S (VA) is their vector sum: S = VI and S² = P² + Q². Example: a load at 100 V rms draws 2 A at power factor 0.6 lagging. P = 100 × 2 × 0.6 = 120 W, S = 200 VA, Q = √(200² − 120²) = 160 var. A parallel capacitor C = Q ÷ (2πfV²) = 160 ÷ (2π × 50 × 100²) = 50.9 µF corrects it to unity at 50 Hz.

sections.heading: Three-phase systems
sections.text: Balanced three-phase voltages are equal in magnitude and 120° apart. In star (Y), line voltage = √3 × phase voltage and line current = phase current. In delta (Δ), line current = √3 × phase current and line voltage = phase voltage. Active power is P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ. The two-wattmeter method measures three-wire power: P = W1 + W2, and for a balanced load Q = √3(W1 − W2).

keyPoints: In sinusoidal steady state, V = IZ with complex impedance; series impedances add and parallel impedances combine like resistors.
For a series RLC circuit, resonance is at f₀ = 1 ÷ (2π√(LC)), where Z = R and current is maximum.
For rms V and I, S = VI, P = VI cos φ, Q = VI sin φ, and S² = P² + Q².
A parallel capacitor C = Q ÷ (2πfV²) supplies reactive power and corrects power factor.
Balanced star: V_L = √3 V_ph and I_L = I_ph; balanced delta: I_L = √3 I_ph and V_L = V_ph.
For balanced three-phase power P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ; two wattmeters give P = W1 + W2 and Q = √3(W1 − W2).

en.title: Semiconductor devices and diode circuits
en.short: PN junction physics, diode characteristics, rectifiers, smoothing, Zener regulators, clippers and other devices.

sections.heading: PN junction
sections.text:
Semiconductor diodes are made from a PN junction: p-type material (with holes, missing electrons) joined to n-type material (with free electrons). Diffusion leaves a depletion region and a barrier potential, about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium.

Forward bias narrows the region and current rises exponentially: I = Is(exp(V ÷ (nVT)) − 1), where VT ≈ 26 mV at room temperature and n is 1 to 2. Reverse bias widens the region and only leakage flows until breakdown.

sections.heading: Rectifiers
sections.text:
Rectifiers convert AC to DC. A half-wave rectifier uses one diode and passes one half-cycle; a full-wave bridge uses four diodes and passes both, giving twice the ripple frequency. A smoothing capacitor charges near the peak and discharges into the load, reducing ripple (the remaining AC variation).

For a 12 V rms, 50 Hz secondary, peak is 12 × √2 = 17.0 V; a bridge drops 1.4 V, leaving 15.6 V. With C = 2200 µF and R = 100 Ω, I = 15.6 ÷ 100 = 0.156 A, so ripple ≈ I ÷ (2fC) = 0.156 ÷ (2 × 50 × 0.0022) = 0.71 V.

sections.heading: Regulation and shaping
sections.text:
A Zener diode works in reverse breakdown and holds a constant voltage. A series resistor drops the excess: I = (Vin − Vz) ÷ Rs. With Vin = 12 V, Vz = 5.1 V and Rs = 220 Ω, current is 6.9 ÷ 220 = 31 mA; a 1 kΩ load takes 5.1 mA, leaving 26 mA in the Zener.

Clippers remove waveform peaks; clampers add a DC level, using diodes with resistors and capacitors.

sections.heading: Other devices
sections.text: Other devices: an LED emits light when forward biased, with colour set by the band gap; a photodiode is reverse biased and produces a photocurrent proportional to light; a thyristor (SCR) latches on when a gate pulse arrives and stays on until its current falls below the holding current. These are used for indication, sensing and power control.

keyPoints: PN junction: forward bias gives exponential conduction; reverse bias blocks until breakdown.
Diode equation: I = Is(exp(V ÷ (nVT)) − 1), with VT ≈ 26 mV at room temperature.
Full-wave bridge rectifiers give twice the ripple frequency of half-wave rectifiers; ripple ≈ I ÷ (2fC) with a smoothing capacitor.
Zener regulator: series resistor current is (Vin − Vz) ÷ Rs, and the Zener takes the current the load does not.
Clippers limit waveform peaks; clampers shift the DC level.
LEDs emit light, photodiodes sense light, and thyristors latch on until current falls below the holding current.

en.title: Transistors and amplifiers
en.short: BJT and FET operation, biasing, small-signal models, CE and CS amplifiers, frequency response and feedback.

sections.heading: Transistor operation
sections.text:
A bipolar junction transistor (BJT) has two junctions. In normal operation the base-emitter junction is forward biased (about 0.7 V for silicon) and the base-collector junction is reverse biased. The collector current is then set by the base current: Ic = βIb, where β is the current gain.

A field-effect transistor (FET) is controlled by voltage. In an n-channel enhancement MOSFET, a gate-source voltage above the threshold Vth opens a channel. In saturation, Id = ½k(Vgs − Vth)².

sections.heading: Biasing and small signals
sections.text:
Biasing sets the quiescent point (Q point): the DC collector current and voltage with no signal applied. The Q point must keep the transistor in the active region over the whole signal swing.

For small signals the transistor becomes a linear model. Transconductance is gm = Ic ÷ VT, with VT ≈ 25 mV at room temperature, and rπ = β ÷ gm.

Example: Ic = 1 mA, so gm = 1 mA ÷ 25 mV = 40 mS. With Rc = 2 kΩ the common-emitter gain is Av = −gm × Rc = −0.04 × 2000 = −80. The minus sign means inversion.

sections.heading: Common source and cascading
sections.text:
The common-source amplifier is the FET counterpart: Av = −gm(Rd ∥ RL), also inverting, with very high input resistance.

Multistage amplifiers cascade stages, so the gains multiply. Capacitive coupling passes the signal but blocks DC, letting each stage be biased separately; direct coupling is used in integrated circuits. Each stage loads the one before it, so loaded gain is lower than unloaded gain.

sections.heading: Frequency response and feedback
sections.text:
Gain falls at high frequency because of internal and stray capacitances; gain times bandwidth is roughly constant. The Miller effect makes a capacitance between input and output appear larger at the input.

Negative feedback returns a fraction of the output to the input in opposition. It divides the gain by about (1 + Aβ), where β here is the feedback fraction, not the transistor current gain. Feedback widens bandwidth and lowers distortion, but can cause instability.

keyPoints: BJT in the active region: Ic = βIb, with the base-emitter junction forward biased.
MOSFET in saturation: Id = ½k(Vgs − Vth)².
Small-signal transconductance: gm = Ic ÷ VT, and rπ = β ÷ gm.
Common-emitter and common-source voltage gain: Av = −gm × (drain or collector resistance in parallel with the load).
Cascaded stage gains multiply; each stage loads the previous one.
Negative feedback trades gain for bandwidth and lower distortion, and can cause instability.

en.title: Operational amplifiers and analogue design
en.short: Ideal and real op-amps, amplifier circuits, filters, comparators and oscillators.

sections.heading: Ideal and practical op-amps
sections.text:
An ideal op-amp has infinite open-loop gain, infinite input impedance, zero output impedance and infinite bandwidth. With negative feedback, the virtual short rule applies: the two inputs sit at almost the same voltage, and no current flows into them.

Practical op-amps have finite gain, input bias and offset currents, offset voltage, finite slew rate and a finite gain-bandwidth product (GBP). The output cannot exceed the supply rails. Open-loop gain falls with frequency, so closed-loop gain and bandwidth trade off.

sections.heading: Amplifier configurations
sections.text:
Inverting amplifier: gain = −Rf ÷ Rin, input impedance Rin, and a virtual earth at the inverting input. Non-inverting: gain = 1 + Rf ÷ Rg, with high input impedance. A summing amplifier gives Vout = −Rf(V1 ÷ R1 + V2 ÷ R2 + ...). A difference amplifier gives Vout = (Rf ÷ Rin)(V2 − V1) when the resistor ratios match.

Example: inverting with Rf = 47 kΩ, Rin = 4.7 kΩ and Vin = 0.2 V. Gain = −47,000 ÷ 4,700 = −10, so Vout = −2.0 V. The same resistors non-inverting give gain 1 + 10 = 11, so Vout = 2.2 V. With ±12 V supplies both outputs stay within the rails.

sections.heading: Integrators, filters, instrumentation
sections.text:
An integrator gives Vout = −(1 ÷ RC) × ∫Vin dt; a feedback resistor limits DC drift. A differentiator gives Vout = −RC × dVin/dt; an input resistor limits noise.

Active filters use op-amps with RC networks; a first-order low-pass has cutoff f = 1 ÷ (2πRC). An instrumentation amplifier uses three op-amps and one gain resistor, giving high common-mode rejection for sensor signals.

sections.heading: Comparators and oscillators
sections.text:
A comparator compares two voltages and drives its output to saturation; positive feedback adds hysteresis (a Schmitt trigger).

A sine-wave oscillator needs loop gain of 1 and 0° phase shift (Barkhausen criterion). The Wien bridge oscillator uses f = 1 ÷ (2πRC) and a non-linear gain control to stabilise amplitude.

keyPoints: Ideal op-amp: infinite gain and input impedance, zero output impedance; with negative feedback the inputs are at equal voltage and draw no current.
Inverting gain is −Rf ÷ Rin; non-inverting gain is 1 + Rf ÷ Rg.
A summing amplifier adds weighted inputs; a difference amplifier subtracts them when resistor ratios match.
Integrator: Vout = −(1 ÷ RC) × ∫Vin dt; differentiator: Vout = −RC × dVin/dt.
First-order active filter cutoff: f = 1 ÷ (2πRC); Wien bridge oscillator frequency: f = 1 ÷ (2πRC).
Practical op-amps have finite gain-bandwidth product, slew rate, offset and bias currents, and output saturation at the supply rails.

en.title: Digital systems and microcontrollers
en.short: Latches, flip-flops, counters, state machines, memory, ADC and DAC, and microcontroller interfacing.

sections.heading: Latches and flip-flops
sections.text:
A latch is a bistable circuit that holds one bit until its inputs change. A transparent D latch passes data while enable is high. A flip-flop samples only on a clock edge, so it changes at that instant, which makes timing predictable.

Setup time is how long data must be steady before the clock edge; hold time is how long after. Violate them and the output may be unpredictable (metastability).

Example: a 1 MHz clock has period 1 ÷ 10⁶ = 1 µs.

sections.heading: Registers, counters, state machines
sections.text:
Registers are groups of flip-flops sharing a clock, holding a word. A shift register moves bits one place per clock.

A counter steps through a fixed sequence; an n-bit binary counter has 2ⁿ states and divides the clock frequency by 2ⁿ.

A finite-state machine (FSM) has states, inputs, outputs and transition rules. In a Moore machine the output depends on the state only; in a Mealy machine it depends on state and input. Draw the state diagram, then encode the states in binary for the flip-flops.

sections.heading: Memory, ADC and DAC
sections.text:
Memory is volatile (loses data without power, as SRAM and DRAM do) or non-volatile (ROM, flash, EEPROM). RAM is random access: any address takes a similar time.

An ADC converts an analogue voltage to a digital code; a DAC does the reverse. An n-bit ADC over a reference range Vref has resolution Vref ÷ 2ⁿ.

Example: 10-bit ADC, Vref = 5 V. Step = 5 ÷ 1024 = 4.88 mV. An input of 2.5 V gives code ≈ 2.5 ÷ 0.00488 = 512.

sections.heading: Microcontrollers and interfacing
sections.text:
A microcontroller is a processor with memory, timers and input/output peripherals on one chip. Embedded programs usually run a loop: read inputs, decide, drive outputs.

A sensor may give an analogue voltage, read through the ADC, or a digital signal over I²C, SPI or UART. An actuator such as a motor or relay needs a driver, because a pin sources only a small current (often tens of mA; check the datasheet).

Case: a tank controller reads a float switch and starts a pump through a relay.

keyPoints: A latch is level-sensitive; a flip-flop changes only on a clock edge and needs data stable for the setup and hold times.
An n-bit binary counter has 2ⁿ states and divides the clock by 2ⁿ.
Moore outputs depend on state only; Mealy outputs depend on state and input.
ADC resolution = Vref ÷ 2ⁿ; a 10-bit, 5 V ADC has a step of 4.88 mV.
SRAM and DRAM are volatile; ROM, flash and EEPROM keep data without power.
Microcontroller pins source small currents, so motors and relays need a driver stage.

en.title: Signals and systems
en.short: Continuous and discrete signals, LTI systems, convolution, Fourier, Laplace, z-transforms, sampling and aliasing.

sections.heading: Signals and systems
sections.text: A signal carries information as a function of time. Continuous-time signals x(t) are defined at every instant; discrete-time signals x[n] exist only at integer indices, often from sampling. A system maps an input signal to an output signal. It is linear if it obeys superposition, time-invariant if a delayed input gives the same delayed output, causal if the output depends only on present and past inputs, and stable if every bounded input gives a bounded output. Memory and invertibility are also properties.

sections.heading: LTI and convolution
sections.text:
A linear time-invariant (LTI) system is fully described by its impulse response h(t) or h[n], the output to a unit impulse. The output is the convolution of input and impulse response:
y(t) = ∫ x(τ)h(t − τ)dτ
y[n] = Σ x[k]h[n − k]
Convolution is commutative and associative. For finite sequences of lengths N and M, the result has length N + M − 1.
Example: x[n] = [1, 2, 1] and h[n] = [1, 1] give y[n] = [1, 3, 3, 1].

sections.heading: Fourier and transforms
sections.text: Fourier series represent a periodic signal as a sum of sinusoids at harmonic frequencies. The Fourier transform extends this idea to non-periodic signals: X(jω) = ∫ x(t)e^(−jωt)dt. It shows the frequency content of a signal. The Laplace transform X(s) = ∫ x(t)e^(−st)dt, with s = σ + jω, handles many signals and initial conditions, and is used to solve linear differential equations. The z-transform X(z) = Σ x[n]z^(−n) is its discrete-time counterpart. State the region of convergence with each transform.

sections.heading: Sampling and aliasing
sections.text: Sampling converts x(t) into x[n] = x(nTs), where Ts is the sampling interval and fs = 1/Ts is the sampling frequency. The Nyquist criterion says fs must be greater than twice the highest signal frequency, fmax, to reconstruct the signal without aliasing. If fs <= 2fmax, high frequencies appear as false lower frequencies. Example: a 1000 Hz cosine sampled at 1500 Hz needs fs > 2000 Hz, so it aliases to 500 Hz.

keyPoints: An LTI system is described by its impulse response, and its output is the convolution of input and impulse response.
Convolution: y(t) = ∫ x(τ)h(t − τ)dτ and y[n] = Σ x[k]h[n − k].
Fourier series apply to periodic signals; the Fourier transform X(jω) = ∫ x(t)e^(−jωt)dt gives frequency content.
Laplace transform X(s) = ∫ x(t)e^(−st)dt and z-transform X(z) = Σ x[n]z^(−n) describe linear systems.
To avoid aliasing, sample above twice the highest frequency: fs > 2fmax.
Linearity, time invariance, causality and stability are key system properties.

en.title: Control systems
en.short: Modelling, transfer functions, block diagrams, stability, root locus, frequency response and PID design.

sections.heading: Modelling and transfer functions
sections.text:
Control systems make an output follow a reference. A linear time-invariant physical system is modelled by an ordinary differential equation. With zero initial conditions, the Laplace transform gives the transfer function G(s) = Y(s) ÷ U(s), the output-to-input ratio in the s-domain.

Example: G(s) = K ÷ (τs + 1) has step response y(t) = K(1 − e^(−t/τ)). With K = 5 and τ = 2 s, at t = 2 s, y = 5(1 − e^(−1)) = 5 × 0.6321 = 3.16.

sections.heading: Block diagrams and stability
sections.text:
Block diagram reduction combines blocks. Series blocks multiply; parallel blocks add. A negative feedback loop with forward path G and feedback H reduces to G ÷ (1 + GH). A signal flow graph shows signals as nodes and gains as branches; Mason’s gain formula gives the overall gain without repeated algebra.

A continuous linear system is stable when all closed-loop poles lie in the left half of the s-plane. Routh-Hurwitz counts right-half-plane roots from the characteristic polynomial by sign changes in the first column of the Routh array.

sections.heading: Root locus and frequency response
sections.text: The root locus plots closed-loop poles as a gain K varies; branches start at open-loop poles and end at open-loop zeros or infinity. Bode plots show magnitude in decibels and phase against frequency. Gain margin and phase margin measure how much gain or phase change is allowed before instability. A Nyquist plot relates encirclements of the −1 point to closed-loop stability.

sections.heading: PID and state space
sections.text: A PID controller uses error e(t): u(t) = Kp e(t) + Ki ∫e dt + Kd de/dt, so C(s) = Kp + Ki ÷ s + Kd s. Proportional action responds to present error, integral action removes steady offset, and derivative action responds to rate of change. Design chooses Kp, Ki and Kd to meet specifications. State space uses xdot = Ax + Bu and y = Cx + Du, where x is the state vector.

keyPoints: A transfer function is G(s) = Y(s) ÷ U(s), found from the linear model with zero initial conditions.
Series blocks multiply, parallel blocks add, and negative feedback reduces to G ÷ (1 + GH).
A continuous linear system is stable only when every closed-loop pole has a negative real part.
Routh-Hurwitz counts right-half-plane roots without solving the characteristic equation.
Root locus, Bode and Nyquist plots show how stability margins change with gain and frequency.
PID control is C(s) = Kp + Ki ÷ s + Kd s; state space is xdot = Ax + Bu, y = Cx + Du.

en.title: Transformers: equivalent circuits, tests and operation
en.short: Construction, equivalent circuits, tests, efficiency, regulation, autotransformers and three-phase operation.

sections.heading: Construction and principle
sections.text: A transformer transfers AC energy between two windings linked by a common magnetic core. The primary takes power; the secondary delivers it. Laminated steel reduces eddy currents. With a sinusoidal supply, induced emf is E = 4.44 f N Φm, where f is frequency, N turns and Φm peak flux. An ideal transformer has no losses or leakage: V1/V2 = N1/N2 = I2/I1.

sections.heading: Equivalent circuit and tests
sections.text: A real transformer is modelled by winding resistance and leakage reactance on each side, plus a shunt branch: Rc for core loss and Xm for magnetising current. Impedances are often referred to one side using the turns ratio squared. The open-circuit test applies rated voltage with the other winding open; it gives core loss and magnetising current. The short-circuit test uses a reduced voltage with the other winding shorted; it gives copper loss and series impedance.

sections.heading: Efficiency and regulation
sections.text: Efficiency η = output power ÷ input power. At load current I and power factor cosφ, output is V I cosφ; losses are core loss Pc (roughly constant) and copper loss I²R (varies with load). Maximum efficiency occurs when copper loss equals core loss. Voltage regulation = (no-load voltage − full-load voltage) ÷ rated voltage × 100%; it is small for a good transformer. Example: 10 kVA transformer at full load, 0.8 pf, core loss 120 W, copper loss 180 W. Output = 10,000 × 0.8 = 8,000 W. Input = 8,000 + 120 + 180 = 8,300 W. η = 8,000 ÷ 8,300 = 0.964, or 96.4%.

sections.heading: Autotransformers and three-phase operation
sections.text: An autotransformer has one tapped winding, so part of the winding is common to input and output. It is smaller and cheaper for a small voltage change but gives no isolation. Three-phase transformers connect windings in star or delta; common arrangements are star-star, delta-delta, star-delta and delta-star. Parallel operation needs the same voltage ratio, polarity and phase displacement, with similar impedances so load shares in proportion to ratings.

keyPoints: Induced emf is E = 4.44 f N Φm for a sinusoidal flux.
An ideal transformer gives V1/V2 = N1/N2 = I2/I1.
A real transformer adds series leakage impedance and a shunt Rc–Xm branch.
The open-circuit test gives core loss; the short-circuit test gives copper loss and series impedance.
Efficiency is output ÷ input; maximum efficiency occurs when copper loss equals core loss.
Parallel transformers need the same voltage ratio, polarity and phase displacement, and similar impedance.

en.title: Rotating electrical machines: DC, induction and synchronous
en.short: Construction, operation, starting, speed control and losses of DC, induction and synchronous machines.

sections.heading: DC machines
sections.text: A DC machine has a field winding or permanent magnets on the stator and an armature winding on the rotor, connected through a commutator and brushes. The commutator reverses armature current so torque stays in one direction. In a motor, back emf E = kΦω opposes the supply, and torque T = kΦIa. A shunt motor runs at nearly constant speed; a series motor gives high starting torque. A starter resistor limits armature current at standstill, when back emf is zero. Speed control uses armature voltage or field flux.

sections.heading: Induction motors
sections.text: A three-phase induction motor has a stator winding that produces a rotating magnetic field at synchronous speed ns = 120f ÷ p rpm, where p is the number of poles. The rotor is a cage or wound type. The field induces rotor currents, and the rotor turns slightly slower than ns. Slip s = (ns − nr) ÷ ns, and rotor frequency is sf. Torque rises with slip up to a maximum. Small motors may start direct-on-line; larger ones use star-delta, autotransformer or soft starting. Speed control uses variable frequency, pole changing or rotor resistance.

sections.heading: Synchronous machines
sections.text: A synchronous machine has a three-phase armature winding on the stator and a DC field winding on the rotor. It runs only at synchronous speed. The field current controls the emf and reactive power, not the speed. It is not self-starting; damper windings or a starter bring it near synchronous speed before field is applied. It can act as a motor or generator.

sections.heading: Losses and example
sections.text: Losses are copper loss I²R, iron loss, mechanical loss and stray loss. Efficiency = output ÷ input. Example: a motor takes 12 kW and loses 1.5 kW, so output is 10.5 kW and efficiency is 10.5 ÷ 12 = 0.875, or 87.5%. At 1,440 rpm its torque is T = P ÷ ω = 10,500 ÷ (2π × 1,440 ÷ 60) = 69.6 N·m.

keyPoints: Back emf in a DC motor is E = kΦω, and torque is T = kΦIa.
Synchronous speed is ns = 120f ÷ p rpm, and slip is s = (ns − nr) ÷ ns.
An induction motor needs slip to induce rotor current and torque.
A synchronous machine runs only at synchronous speed; field current controls reactive power.
Efficiency = output ÷ input, and torque T = P ÷ ω with ω in rad/s.
Starting methods limit current; speed control changes voltage, frequency, poles or rotor resistance.

en.title: Power electronics and electric drives
en.short: Switching devices, rectifiers, choppers, inverters, PWM and their use in electric drives.

sections.heading: Devices and switching
sections.text: Power semiconductor devices act as controlled switches. A diode conducts one way only and is uncontrolled. A thyristor (SCR) latches on with a gate pulse and turns off when current falls below the holding level. A metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) switches fast at low voltage; an insulated-gate bipolar transistor (IGBT) combines an insulated gate with bipolar conduction for higher power. Switching is not ideal: turn-on and turn-off take time, and energy is lost in switching and conduction. Ratings must be respected.

sections.heading: Rectifiers and choppers
sections.text: A rectifier converts AC to DC. Uncontrolled rectifiers use diodes; controlled rectifiers use thyristors and delay firing by angle alpha, so the average output falls as alpha increases. A DC chopper converts fixed DC to variable DC by switching. In a buck chopper the average output is Vout = D × Vin, where D is the duty cycle. Example: Vin = 48 V and D = 0.4 give Vout = 0.4 × 48 = 19.2 V. Boost and buck-boost choppers give other ratios.

sections.heading: Inverters and PWM
sections.text: An inverter converts DC to AC. A square-wave inverter is simple but produces strong harmonics. Pulse width modulation (PWM) switches many times per cycle and varies pulse widths to synthesise a sinusoidal fundamental. A higher switching frequency moves harmonics to higher frequencies, making filtering easier, but increases switching losses. AC voltage controllers vary the RMS AC voltage by phase control or integral-cycle control; they are used for lamp dimming and soft starting.

sections.heading: Electric drives
sections.text: An electric drive is a motor, converter, controller and load working together. Rectifiers feed DC links; choppers control DC motors; inverters feed induction and synchronous machines with variable voltage and frequency. For an induction motor, synchronous speed is ns = 120f ÷ p, where p is the number of poles, so changing frequency changes speed; voltage is adjusted with frequency to keep flux near constant. Closed-loop control regulates torque or speed. Regenerative braking returns energy where the converter allows it. Installation rules differ by country; check the local code.

keyPoints: Power semiconductor devices are switches; a diode is uncontrolled and a thyristor latches on until current falls below the holding level.
A controlled rectifier delays firing by angle alpha, so its average DC output falls as alpha increases.
A buck chopper gives Vout = D × Vin, where D is the duty cycle.
An inverter converts DC to AC; PWM shapes the output toward a sine wave and moves harmonics to higher frequencies.
For an induction motor, synchronous speed is ns = 120f ÷ p, with p the number of poles.
Drive converters must respect device ratings and local installation rules, which differ by country.

en.title: Power systems analysis and protection
en.short: Covers generation, transmission, per-unit, load flow, faults, relays, breakers and earthing.

sections.heading: System structure
sections.text: Electric power systems generate at power stations, step voltage up for transmission, carry bulk power on high-voltage lines, then step down through distribution networks to consumers. Generation, transmission and distribution are linked by transformers; transmission is meshed for reliability, distribution is often radial. Voltages and practices differ by country, so use the local code and note professional registration, for example COREN in Nigeria.

sections.heading: Per unit and lines
sections.text: Per-unit quantities remove voltage-level differences. Choose base power Sbase and base voltage Vbase; then Ibase = Sbase ÷ (√3 Vbase), Zbase = Vbase² ÷ Sbase. A quantity in per unit is actual ÷ base. Transmission-line parameters are resistance R, inductance L and capacitance C, usually given per unit length; series impedance is R + jωL and shunt admittance jωC. Example: on 100 MVA and 132 kV bases, Zbase = 132² ÷ 100 = 174.24 Ω. A 20 Ω line is 20 ÷ 174.24 = 0.115 pu.

sections.heading: Load flow and faults
sections.text: Load flow (power flow) solves bus voltages and power flows for specified generation and loads. It uses nodal equations, often Newton-Raphson. Symmetrical fault analysis finds three-phase short-circuit current using per-unit reactances and a Thevenin equivalent. Example: a 1.0 pu voltage source behind 0.20 pu reactance gives I = 1.0 ÷ 0.20 = 5.0 pu. On the same 100 MVA, 132 kV base, Ibase = 100 × 10⁶ ÷ (√3 × 132 × 10³) = 437.4 A, so fault current = 5.0 × 437.4 = 2,187 A.

sections.heading: Protection and earthing
sections.text: Protection relays detect abnormal current, voltage or frequency and trip circuit breakers to isolate faults. Overcurrent, distance and differential schemes are common; coordination ensures the nearest breaker clears the fault. Circuit breakers interrupt fault current, and their rating must exceed the prospective fault level. Earthing provides a low-impedance path and controls touch voltage; methods and limits vary by country and installation type, so check the local wiring regulations. In Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering registration, but installation rules are separate.

keyPoints: Per-unit values use common Sbase and Vbase; Ibase = Sbase ÷ (√3 Vbase) and Zbase = Vbase² ÷ Sbase.
Transmission lines are modelled by series R + jωL and shunt jωC, usually per unit length.
Load flow solves bus voltages and power flows; Newton-Raphson is a common method.
Symmetrical fault current is V ÷ Z from the Thevenin equivalent in per unit.
Protection relays detect faults and trip circuit breakers; coordination limits outages.
Earthing and protection limits vary by country and installation, so check local regulations and registration, such as COREN in Nigeria.

en.title: Electrical installation design and wiring regulations
en.short: Domestic and industrial wiring, load estimation, cable sizing, voltage drop, protection and earthing.

sections.heading: Wiring systems
sections.text: Domestic installations commonly use PVC-insulated cables in conduit or twin-and-earth cable. Industrial work uses armoured or screened multicore cables on tray or in trunking, with isolation and labelling. Select wiring for heat, water, corrosion and mechanical damage. A wiring system includes conductors, enclosures, joints, accessories and support.

sections.heading: Load estimation
sections.text: Load estimation begins with connected load: add the rated power of every appliance and circuit. Apply diversity, a factor allowing for equipment not all running at once, to obtain maximum demand and design current Ib. Single-phase: Ib = P ÷ (V × power factor). Balanced three-phase: Ib = P ÷ (√3 × VL × power factor). Diversity factors vary; use the current wiring regulations or documented good practice.

sections.heading: Cable sizing and voltage drop
sections.text:
Cable size must satisfy Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz. In is the protective device rating; Iz is the cable current-carrying capacity after correction for ambient temperature, grouping and installation method. Voltage drop: drop = mV/A/m × Ib × length ÷ 1000.

Example: Ib = 20 A, length = 30 m, mV/A/m = 18. Drop = 18 × 20 × 30 ÷ 1000 = 10.8 V. On 230 V this is 10.8 ÷ 230 × 100 = 4.7 per cent. Check the limit in the current edition.

sections.heading: Protection, earthing and regulations
sections.text:
Fuses and miniature circuit breakers (MCBs) clear overloads and short circuits. A residual current device (RCD) detects earth leakage and disconnects the supply. Earthing connects exposed metalwork to earth so fault current trips the device; protective bonding reduces touch voltage.

In Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering registration, and installation design follows national regulations and standards. Designers often refer to the IET Wiring Regulations (BS 7671), but must confirm the edition and local amendments. Other countries have their own codes.

keyPoints: Design current for single phase is Ib = P ÷ (V × power factor); for balanced three phase it is Ib = P ÷ (√3 × VL × power factor).
Cable selection requires Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz, with Iz corrected for installation conditions.
Voltage drop = mV/A/m × Ib × length ÷ 1000.
Protective devices must clear faults; RCDs detect earth leakage.
Earthing and bonding limit touch voltage and help fault current operate protection.
Wiring regulations and registration rules differ by country; always check the current edition and local requirements.

en.title: Communication systems and electromagnetic waves
en.short: AM, FM, noise, receivers, digital modulation, transmission lines, antennas and link budgets.

sections.heading: Modulation
sections.text: Modulation places a message on a carrier. In amplitude modulation (AM) the carrier amplitude follows the message; in frequency modulation (FM) the carrier frequency shifts. AM is simple and narrowband but sensitive to amplitude noise. FM has constant amplitude, so it resists amplitude noise but uses more bandwidth. For AM with a single tone, the sidebands lie at fc ± fm.

sections.heading: Noise and receivers
sections.text: Noise is unwanted energy. Thermal noise power is Pn = kTB, where k is Boltzmann’s constant, T absolute temperature and B bandwidth. At T = 290 K and B = 1 MHz, Pn ≈ 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ W = −114 dBm. A receiver must raise the signal above noise. A superheterodyne receiver mixes the signal to a fixed intermediate frequency (IF), filters and amplifies it, then demodulates. Selectivity rejects adjacent channels; sensitivity is the weakest usable signal; noise figure measures added noise.

sections.heading: Digital modulation
sections.text: Digital modulation maps bits to carrier states. Amplitude shift keying (ASK) changes amplitude, frequency shift keying (FSK) changes frequency, and phase shift keying (PSK) changes phase. Quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) combines amplitude and phase, sending more bits per symbol but needing a higher signal-to-noise ratio. Rb = Rs log2 M, where M is the number of symbols.

sections.heading: Lines, antennas and links
sections.text: A transmission line carries guided waves; characteristic impedance Z0 and termination decide reflection. A matched load absorbs all power; mismatch causes standing waves, measured by voltage standing wave ratio (VSWR). Radio waves propagate by ground, sky and space waves; higher frequencies need line of sight. An antenna converts guided waves to radiated waves; gain in dBi compares it with an isotropic radiator. A link budget adds gains and subtracts losses: Pr = Pt + Gt + Gr − L. Example: Pt = 40 dBm, Gt = 10 dBi, Gr = 0 dBi, cable loss 2 dB, path loss 120 dB. Then Pr = 40 + 10 + 0 − 2 − 120 = −72 dBm. With sensitivity −90 dBm, margin is 18 dB.

keyPoints: AM varies carrier amplitude; FM varies carrier frequency.
FM resists amplitude noise but needs more bandwidth than AM.
Thermal noise power is Pn = kTB; at 290 K and 1 MHz it is about −114 dBm.
A superheterodyne receiver mixes to an intermediate frequency, then filters, amplifies and demodulates.
Digital modulation maps bits to symbols; Rb = Rs log2 M.
Link budget: Pr = Pt + Gt + Gr − L; margin = Pr − sensitivity.

en.title: Digital signal processing: DFT, FFT and digital filters
en.short: Discrete-time signals, the DFT and FFT, FIR and IIR filter design, windowing and spectral analysis.

sections.heading: Discrete-time basics
sections.text: A discrete-time signal is a sequence x[n], with integer sample index n. If x(t) is sampled every T seconds, x[n] = x(nT). Frequency is Ω radians per sample, where Ω = 2πfT. A linear time-invariant (LTI) system is described by its impulse response h[n]. Its output is the convolution y[n] = Σ h[k]x[n−k]. Recursive difference equations, such as y[n] = a x[n] + b y[n−1], need stability checks: an LTI system is stable when Σ |h[n]| is finite.

sections.heading: DFT and FFT
sections.text: The discrete Fourier transform (DFT) maps N samples to N frequency coefficients: X[k] = Σ x[n] e^(−j2πkn/N), summed over n = 0 to N−1. The inverse DFT returns x[n]. The fast Fourier transform (FFT) computes the same values in about N log₂N operations instead of N². Example: x = [1, 0, −1, 0] gives X = [0, 2, 0, 2]. The DFT assumes periodicity, so multiplying DFTs filters by circular convolution unless zero padding is used.

sections.heading: FIR and IIR filters
sections.text: An FIR filter has a finite impulse response, so it is always stable and can have exact linear phase when symmetric. Example: y[n] = 0.5x[n] + 0.5x[n−1] has gain 1 at zero frequency and 0 at the Nyquist frequency (half the sampling rate). An IIR filter uses feedback, so it can meet a specification with fewer coefficients but may be unstable; its poles must lie inside the unit circle. A common design route is an analogue prototype followed by the bilinear transform, which warps frequency, so critical frequencies are pre-warped.

sections.heading: Windowing and spectra
sections.text: Windowing multiplies a finite record by a taper, such as Hann or Hamming, to reduce spectral leakage from abrupt ends. A wider main lobe gives poorer frequency resolution; lower side lobes give less leakage. For N samples at sampling rate fs, DFT bin spacing is fs/N. Averaging spectra reduces random noise. Zero padding interpolates the spectrum but does not improve true resolution.

keyPoints: An LTI system is described by h[n], and y[n] = Σ h[k]x[n−k].
The DFT is X[k] = Σ x[n] e^(−j2πkn/N), and the FFT reduces the operation count to about N log₂N.
An FIR filter is always stable and can have exact linear phase when its coefficients are symmetric.
An IIR filter uses feedback, so its poles must lie inside the unit circle for stability.
The bilinear transform maps analogue designs to IIR filters but warps frequency, so pre-warp critical frequencies.
Windowing trades main-lobe width against side-lobe level; DFT bin spacing is fs/N.

en.title: Renewable energy and distributed generation
en.short: Solar, wind, small hydro and biomass, their resource assessment, conversion, storage and grid integration.

sections.heading: Resource assessment
sections.text: Resource assessment estimates how much energy a site can supply. For solar, measure daily insolation in kWh/m² per day and temperature; for wind, measure speed and direction over at least a year, because power rises with the cube of speed. For small hydro, find flow Q in m³/s and head H in metres. For biomass, find dry tonnes per year, moisture and calorific value. Capacity factor is average output divided by rated output; it compares sites and technologies fairly.

sections.heading: Conversion
sections.text: Solar photovoltaic (PV) cells convert light directly to DC electricity; maximum power point tracking (MPPT) keeps the array near its best operating point. Wind turbines turn a generator through a gearbox or direct drive; small hydro uses a turbine and generator; biomass is burned, gasified or digested to drive a generator or engine. Example: a wind turbine with rotor diameter 20 m, wind speed 8 m/s, air density 1.225 kg/m³ and power coefficient 0.40. Area = π × 10² = 314.2 m². P = 0.5 × ρ × A × v³ × Cp = 0.5 × 1.225 × 314.2 × 8³ × 0.40 = 39.4 kW.

sections.heading: Inverters and storage
sections.text: PV and many small generators produce DC or variable-frequency AC, so power converters are needed. A grid-tied inverter synchronises its output with the grid, controls current and must disconnect safely when the grid is lost (anti-islanding). Batteries, pumped hydro and flywheels store energy; their energy capacity (kWh) and power rating (kW) are separate. Storage smooths output, shifts energy and supports voltage and frequency.

sections.heading: Distributed generation issues
sections.text: Distributed generation (DG) is generation connected near load rather than at large central stations. It can reduce losses, but many small sources create technical issues: voltage rise on feeders, reverse power flow, higher fault levels, protection miscoordination, harmonics from inverters, and islanding risk. Grid codes set limits for voltage, frequency, power factor and protection; these differ by country, so check the current national code and utility rules.

keyPoints: Solar resource is measured as daily insolation in kWh/m² per day; wind power varies with the cube of wind speed.
Wind power: P = 0.5 × ρ × A × v³ × Cp, where Cp is the power coefficient.
Small hydro power: P = ρ × g × Q × H × η, where η is efficiency.
Capacity factor = average output ÷ rated output.
Grid-tied inverters must synchronise, control power quality and provide anti-islanding protection.
DG can cause voltage rise, reverse power, fault-level and protection problems; limits are set by national grid codes.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and project management
en.short: Engineering economics, project planning, professional ethics and reporting a final-year project.

sections.heading: Engineering economics
sections.text:
Engineering economics compares alternatives by cash flow over time. Payback period is the time for cumulative savings to repay the initial cost; it ignores later cash and the time value of money. Net present value (NPV) discounts each cash flow Ct at rate r: NPV = −C0 + Σ Ct ÷ (1 + r)^t. A positive NPV adds value; choose the higher NPV when only one option can be chosen.

Example: a project costs 10,000 and saves 3,000 a year for 4 years. At r = 10%, the annuity factor is (1 − 1.1⁻⁴) ÷ 0.1 = 3.1699. NPV = −10,000 + 3,000 × 3.1699 = −490. Payback is 3.33 years, but the negative NPV says reject at 10%.

sections.heading: Project planning
sections.text: A Gantt chart draws tasks as bars against time, so progress and overlaps are visible. A critical path method (CPM) network shows dependencies explicitly. The critical path is the longest path through the network; its duration is the shortest project duration. Tasks on it have zero float (slack), so delay delays completion. Float is the time a task can slip without affecting the finish. Use Gantt charts for communication and CPM for scheduling logic.

sections.heading: Ethics and standards
sections.text: Professional ethics require honesty, competence, public safety, confidentiality and disclosure of conflicts of interest. Codes and standards are agreed technical rules; their legal status varies, so name the country and check the current edition. Registration also differs. In Nigeria, COREN (the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria) regulates engineering registration. The IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) is an international technical professional association, and the IET (Institution of Engineering and Technology) is a UK professional engineering institution; statutory registration or chartered status comes through national systems, not automatically from membership. Verify current requirements with the official body.

sections.heading: Final-year report
sections.text: A final-year project report normally has a title, abstract, introduction with aims, literature review, method, results, discussion, conclusion, references and appendices. Report what you did, show enough data for another person to repeat it, cite sources, acknowledge help and avoid plagiarism. Follow your department’s format and submission rules.

keyPoints: Payback period is the time for cumulative savings to repay the initial cost.
NPV = −C0 + Σ Ct ÷ (1 + r)^t; accept a project with positive NPV at the chosen rate.
The critical path is the longest path in the network, has zero float, and sets the shortest project duration.
Professional ethics require honesty, competence, public safety and disclosure of conflicts of interest.
Codes and registration differ by country; in Nigeria COREN regulates engineering registration, while IEEE and IET are professional bodies, not automatic licences.
A final-year report must state aims, method, results and conclusions honestly, cite sources and be reproducible.

en.title: Advanced power systems analysis and stability
en.short: Power flow, symmetrical components, fault analysis, stability, control and smart-grid operation.

sections.heading: Power flow
sections.text: AC power flow finds bus voltage magnitudes and angles that balance P and Q. Bus types are slack (reference), PV (voltage controlled) and PQ (load). Newton-Raphson uses a Jacobian and converges quadratically; Gauss-Seidel is simpler but slower. Fast-decoupled methods exploit weak P-V and Q-angle coupling. The DC approximation assumes small angles and negligible resistance, giving P ≈ Bθ.

sections.heading: Fault analysis
sections.text:
Symmetrical components resolve an unbalanced three-phase set into positive, negative and zero sequences. With a = 1∠120°, Va = V0 + V1 + V2, Vb = V0 + a²V1 + aV2 and Vc = V0 + aV1 + a²V2. The inverse is V0 = (Va + Vb + Vc) ÷ 3, V1 = (Va + aVb + a²Vc) ÷ 3 and V2 = (Va + a²Vb + aVc) ÷ 3.

Fault analysis connects sequence networks by fault type. A three-phase fault uses positive sequence only; a line-to-ground fault uses all three in series. Example: Va = 100 V, Vb = Vc = −50 V gives V0 = 0, V1 = 50 V, V2 = 50 V.

sections.heading: Stability
sections.text: Steady-state stability concerns small disturbances. For a lossless line, P = (EV ÷ X) sin δ; the synchronising coefficient is dP ÷ dδ = (EV ÷ X) cos δ. Transient stability concerns large disturbances and uses the swing equation (2H ÷ ωs) d²δ ÷ dt² = Pm − Pe per unit, where H is the inertia constant. The equal area criterion gives the critical clearing angle for one machine on an infinite bus.

sections.heading: Control and smart grids
sections.text: Excitation control through an automatic voltage regulator holds terminal voltage; a power system stabiliser adds damping. Turbine governors use speed droop for primary frequency response, and secondary control restores frequency. Smart-grid operation adds distributed generation, microgrids, demand response, metering and communication, with state estimation and cybersecurity. Limits and registration rules differ by country; check the local grid code and regulator.

keyPoints: Newton-Raphson power flow uses a Jacobian and converges quadratically; the DC approximation is P ≈ Bθ.
Symmetrical components use a = 1∠120°, with Va = V0 + V1 + V2, Vb = V0 + a²V1 + aV2 and Vc = V0 + aV1 + a²V2.
Sequence networks are connected according to fault type; a single line-to-ground fault uses all three sequences in series.
Steady-state power transfer is P = (EV ÷ X) sin δ, with maximum at δ = 90° for a lossless line.
The swing equation (2H ÷ ωs) d²δ ÷ dt² = Pm − Pe describes transient rotor angle stability.
Excitation and turbine controls support voltage and frequency; smart-grid limits and registration rules vary by country.

en.title: Advanced control systems
en.short: State-space models, controllability, observers, LQR, robust and nonlinear control, and digital control.

sections.heading: State-space models
sections.text:
A state-space model uses first-order equations: xdot = Ax + Bu, y = Cx + Du. The state vector x holds the variables that, with future inputs, determine future behaviour. For a linear time-invariant system, A, B, C and D are constant matrices. The eigenvalues of A are the poles and set stability and speed.

Example: A = [0 1; −3 −2]. Its eigenvalues solve λ² + 2λ + 3 = 0, so λ = −1 ± j√2. The real part is negative, so the system is stable.

sections.heading: Controllability and observers
